records.sourceFile: Load-velocity relationship variables to assess the maximal neuromuscular capacities during the back squat exercise.pdf

paper.citation: Pérez-Castilla A, Jukic I, Janicijevic D, Akyildiz Z, Senturk D, García-Ramos A. Load-Velocity Relationship Variables to Assess the Maximal Neuromuscular Capacities During the Back-Squat Exercise. Sports Health. 2022.
paper.abstract: Twenty-four male national-level wrestlers completed 1RM and load-velocity testing during concentric-only and eccentric-concentric back squats on a Smith machine. Aline was highly reliable, L0 and v0 had acceptable CVs but lower ICCs, and L0 and Aline were strongly associated with 1RM and Pmax. The authors conclude that load-velocity variables are a quick, simple estimate of maximal force and power capacity during the back squat.
paper.tldr: A short load-velocity test on the back squat gave reliable estimates of maximal strength and power in national-level male wrestlers. The area under the line (Aline) was the most reliable variable, and the velocity-axis intercept (v0) was the least reliable.
paper.methods: Twenty-four male wrestlers completed a 1RM session and four experimental sessions (two concentric-only and two eccentric-concentric back squats) on a Smith machine, with at least 48 hours between sessions. Each session used 3 repetitions at 45%, 55%, 65%, 75% and 85% of 1RM, followed by 1RM attempts, with velocity recorded by a linear position transducer. Reliability was assessed with CV and ICC between sessions, and validity with correlations of L0 with 1RM and of Aline with Pmax.
paper.findings: Aline had high between-session reliability (CV 2.58% to 4.37%; ICC 0.97 to 0.99, Table 1). L0 (CV 5.25% to 9.01%; ICC 0.77 to 0.91) and v0 (CV 5.08% to 8.66%; ICC 0.45 to 0.72) had CVs within the acceptable range, but all v0 ICCs and the eccentric-concentric average-score L0 ICC were below 0.80 and are flagged in Table 1 as unacceptable; no significant between-session differences were found (P >= 0.23). L0 correlated very largely with 1RM (r = 0.87 to 0.88) and Aline nearly perfectly with Pmax (r = 0.98 to 0.99; all P < 0.001), and all three variables were more reliable with the concentric-only variant (CV ratio 1.49 to 1.65).
paper.limitations: The sample was 24 male national-level wrestlers (age 19.1 +/- 3.4 years, some under 18) tested on a Smith machine, which restricts the bar to vertical movement and may limit generalizability to free-weight squatting and other athletes. The abstract gives ICC ranges of 0.98 to 0.99 for Aline and 0.45 to 0.96 for L0 and v0, but Table 1 gives 0.97 to 0.99 and 0.45 to 0.91, so table values are reported here. The authors call L0 and v0 reliability acceptable, but by their own stated criteria (ICC >= 0.80) v0 ICCs were unacceptable in every condition; v0 validity was not tested and L-V variables lack a clear physiological meaning.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use L0 and Aline from a Smith-machine back squat load-velocity profile as a quick estimate of maximal strength and power. The concentric-only variant gave more reliable values for all three variables, and v0 should not be tracked on its own given ICCs of 0.45 to 0.72.
paper.athleteDev: The load-velocity profile can estimate maximal strength (L0) and maximal power (Aline) in male athletes using only velocity data and a few submaximal loads. Changes in v0 are less reproducible here (ICC 0.45 to 0.72), so they should not be used alone to judge training effects.
paper.rtp: The study tested healthy wrestlers and did not assess injured athletes or rehabilitation outcomes, so it cannot be used to judge return-to-sport readiness.

records.sourceFile: Low Ankle-GO Score while returning to sport after lateral ankle sprain leads to a 9-fold increased risk of recurrence - A two-year prospective cohort study.pdf

paper.citation: Picot B, Fourchet F, Lopes R, Rauline G, Freiha K, D'hooghe P, et al. Low Ankle-GO Score While Returning to Sport After Lateral Ankle Sprain Leads to a 9-fold Increased Risk of Recurrence: A Two-year Prospective Cohort Study. Sports Medicine - Open. 2024;10:23.
paper.abstract: In 54 of 64 active patients followed for two years after a lateral ankle sprain, a two-month Ankle-GO score was lower in those who had a recurrent sprain (5.4 vs 9.1 points, p = 0.002; AUC 0.75). A score below 8 points was associated with higher recurrence odds (OR 8.6, 95% CI 2 to 37.2) in multivariable logistic regression. The authors report a non-significant trend toward higher recurrence in women (OR 3.8, 95% CI 0.9 to 15.5, p = 0.065).
paper.tldr: A low Ankle-GO score two months after a lateral ankle sprain was associated with a later recurrence in this small cohort. Scores below 8 points gave an odds ratio of about 9 for recurrence, but the estimate is imprecise and has not been tested in a separate sample.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort. Sixty-four active patients with a recent lateral ankle sprain completed the Ankle-GO score, which combines two questionnaires and four functional tests for 25 points, about two months after injury. Two years later a blinded assessor asked about recurrence, and 54 responded. Groups were compared with chi-square, t and Mann-Whitney tests, a Youden-index cut-off was derived, and stepwise logistic regression was used.
paper.findings: Eighteen of 54 (33.3%) had a recurrent sprain, all non-contact. The two-month Ankle-GO score was 5.4 +/- 2.8 points in patients with recurrence and 9.1 +/- 4.5 without (p = 0.002), with AUC 0.75 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.88). The 8-point cut-off gave 83% sensitivity and 64% specificity. In the multivariable model the score was the only significant predictor, with OR 8.6 (95% CI 2 to 37.2) for a score below 8 points.
paper.limitations: Only 18 recurrences, a cut-off chosen on the same data, and 15% loss to follow-up limit precision and generalisability. The nine-fold figure is an odds ratio, not a risk ratio. The p value for the odds ratio is 0.001 in the abstract and 0.004 in the results. Sex labels conflict: Methods give 36 women and 28 men, Table 1 header gives men/women as 36/28, and Table 3 lists 4 women and 14 men among reinjured patients. On the Table 3 counts, the reinjury proportion was lower in women (4 of 23) than in men (14 of 31), which contradicts the authors' sex conclusion; the reported women OR of 3.8 (95% CI 0.9 to 15.5, p = 0.065) is not significant. Rehabilitation content, injury severity and other known risk factors were not analysed.
paper.practicalImplications: Use the Ankle-GO as one objective input alongside clinical judgement when deciding return to sport, rather than as a threshold that clears or blocks an athlete. A low score at two months may justify closer follow-up and rehabilitation of the deficits the patients showed, such as the SEBT and FAAM-ADL results, but an 8-point cut-off needs external validation before it is used as a fixed rule.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The study measured recurrence, not performance, so it does not show that the score predicts athletic performance. It may help identify which balance and hop deficits to address during late-stage rehabilitation.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: A score below 8 points at two months was associated with later recurrence, so it may flag athletes who benefit from further rehabilitation before full return. The study cannot show that a score of 8 or above makes return safe, and it does not establish a validated clearance threshold.

records.sourceFile: MRI radiomics for hamstring stain injury identification and return to sport classification - A pilot study.pdf

paper.citation: Torres-Velazquez M, Wille CM, Hurley SA, Kijowski R, Heiderscheit BC, McMillan AB. MRI radiomics for hamstring strain injury identification and return to sport classification: a pilot study. Skeletal Radiol. 2023.
paper.abstract: This pilot study tested whether MRI radiomics from the hamstring muscles of 32 collegiate athletes with a hamstring strain injury can separate injured from uninjured limbs and classify time to return to sport. Support vector classifiers were cross-validated using DTI, T2-weighted and T1-weighted features, and the best-performing combinations were reported for each task.
paper.tldr: In a 32-athlete pilot, MRI radiomics features classified injured limbs and return-to-sport timing well in cross-validation. The approach is unvalidated on an external sample, so it is not ready for clinical decisions.
paper.methods: MRI from 32 collegiate athletes (2017-2020) with an acute hamstring strain was analyzed, using T1-weighted, T2-weighted and diffusion tensor imaging, with four hamstring muscles segmented in each limb. A total of 101 PyRadiomics features per muscle and modality were extracted and fed to L1-penalized logistic regression feature selection (up to 25 features) and a radial basis function support vector classifier. Performance was assessed with 10-fold (binary) or 7-fold (multiclass) cross-validation repeated 10 times, using accuracy, AUC and weighted F1 scores; return to sport was defined by medical clearance, split at 25 days for the binary task and into under 14, 14 to 42 and over 42 days for the multiclass task.
paper.findings: For involved versus uninvolved limbs, combined DTI and T2w features gave the highest mean test accuracy (0.842, SD 0.163) and AUC (0.844, SD 0.163), but were not significantly better than all DTI features or all features combined. For the binary return-to-sport task at 25 days (16 athletes per group), all radiomics combined gave accuracy 0.953 (SD 0.158) and AUC 0.958 (SD 0.150), and DTI alone gave accuracy 0.933. For the three-class task (7, 14 and 11 athletes), DTI features gave the highest weighted one-vs-rest AUC (0.809, SD 0.162); Table 4 prints a weighted F1 of 0.721 (SD 0.227) for this model, while the results text prints 0.93 (SD 0.19).
paper.limitations: The sample was small (n = 32), and the authors acknowledge overfitting risk because there was no separate test dataset; the 25-day cutoff was chosen to balance groups and the multiclass groups were very small. Clinical return-to-sport tests were not compared, and the authors note clearance-based return to sport may be premature. The text has internal conflicts: the multiclass weighted F1 is 0.93 in the text but 0.721 in Table 4, the 14 to 42 day class is labelled '2-4 weeks', and Table 1 lists 26 primary injured muscles although 28 athletes had a BAMIC grade above 0.
paper.practicalImplications: Radiomics should not be used to set return-to-sport dates for individual athletes on the basis of this study. Clinicians may note that MRI texture features from DTI and T2-weighted images separated injured from uninjured limbs in this cohort, and that larger, longitudinal datasets are needed before any clinical use.
paper.athleteDev: This paper does not address training or performance. Its MRI features are not a validated performance or readiness measure and should not be used as one.
paper.rtp: The study models time to return to sport, but only in cross-validation on 32 athletes, with clearance timing as the reference standard. It cannot be used to guide return-to-play decisions and provides no comparison with clinical return-to-sport tests.

records.sourceFile: Maximal Strength in Relation to Force and Velocity Patterns During Countermovement Jumps.pdf

paper.citation: Haischer MH, Krzyszkowski J, Roche S, Kipp K. Maximal Strength in Relation to Force and Velocity Patterns During Countermovement Jumps. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2021.
paper.abstract: The study examined how isometric midthigh pull peak force relates to time-series patterns of ground reaction force and center-of-mass velocity during countermovement jumps in female college lacrosse players. Principal components analysis was used to extract the patterns from the full jump waveforms.
paper.tldr: In 19 female collegiate lacrosse players, stronger athletes showed countermovement jump patterns with higher eccentric rate of force development and higher peak force, while jump height did not correlate with strength. Waveform patterns may be more informative than discrete variables, but this needs replication.
paper.methods: Nineteen female Division I lacrosse players completed up to three maximal countermovement jumps and three maximal isometric midthigh pulls in one session at the start of an off-season period. Force-plate data were time-normalized to 101 points and analysed by principal components analysis, and Spearman correlations with bootstrapped 95% CIs linked midthigh pull peak force to discrete jump variables and principal component scores.
paper.findings: Midthigh pull peak force correlated with a ground reaction force pattern (PC2, rho 0.544, P = .016) that reflected higher eccentric rate of force development, higher peak force and a unimodal profile. It also correlated with a center-of-mass velocity pattern (PC2, rho 0.634, P = .004) that reflected higher concentric velocity, while it did not correlate with jump height (rho 0.308, P = .199) or other discrete jump variables.
paper.limitations: The sample is 19 women from one team, the design is cross-sectional, and the authors state it is unknown whether the relationships change over a season or with training. The paper describes no correction for the many correlations tested, and the authors note that linear time normalization could change results.
paper.practicalImplications: Coaches who test strength with the midthigh pull may find that jump waveform patterns relate to strength when jump height does not, so waveform analysis may add information to jump monitoring. The authors suggest the findings frame directional hypotheses for training studies rather than settled measures.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can consider force-plate waveform analysis alongside peak-force testing to see how athletes produce jumps, which the authors suggest may help monitor change. The study does not test whether these patterns change with training or fatigue.
paper.rtp: The study includes no injured athletes and does not address return to sport. Its jump waveform patterns have no established return-to-play thresholds.

records.sourceFile: Mechanical and metabolic power in accelerated running - Part 2 - Team sports.pdf

paper.citation: Osgnach C, di Prampero PE, Zamparo P, Morin JB, Pavei G. Mechanical and metabolic power in accelerated running Part II: team sports. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2024;124:417-431.
paper.abstract: The authors discuss how velocity and acceleration together set mechanical and metabolic power in team sports. They use GPS data from 38 official matches of one Italian Serie B team to compare acceleration-count and power-based event counts, and they track metabolic power events across 15-minute periods.
paper.tldr: Counting accelerations above a fixed 2.5 m/s2 threshold undercounts high-intensity efforts, and the undercount differs by position. Power-based and metabolic event counts describe match demands more completely, but they come from one team in one season.
paper.methods: Retrospective analysis of GPS data sampled at 18.18 Hz from 29 outfield players (549 match observations) over 38 official matches. Individual acceleration-speed profiles were built in situ from match data (320 profiles from 24 players; role averages for the other 5), and events were counted when external power exceeded 80% of each player's estimated maximal power (#burst) and when metabolic power exceeded an assumed VO2max of 18 W/kg (#MPE).
paper.findings: For players who completed the full match, mechanical power events were 1.61 times the number of acceleration events above 2.5 m/s2 (2.30 for midfielders and 1.36 for attackers). Metabolic power events averaged 151.9 per match, and in full-match players their number fell from 28.1 to 21.4 per 15-minute period while the recovery between them rose from 25.5 s to 36.5 s.
paper.limitations: The study covers one team and one season, with retrospective data and no outcome validation against performance or injury. The authors acknowledge that substitutions and tactical changes affect the late-match trends, and the thresholds (80% of maximal power, 2.5 m/s2, an assumed 18 W/kg for VO2max) were chosen by the authors. Two authors are scientific consultants for the company that supplied the GPS units.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff profiling match demands should not rely on acceleration counts alone, because those counts undercount intense efforts unevenly across positions. Mechanical and metabolic power counts can be reported alongside them, with the threshold choices stated. Results from one squad should not be used as positional norms for other teams.
paper.athleteDev: Use power-based event counts alongside acceleration counts when describing match demands by position, and compare each player with their own acceleration-speed profile rather than with a fixed threshold.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It describes match demands in professional players and gives no clinical or return-to-play criteria.

records.sourceFile: Metabolic Power in Team Sports - Part 1- An Update.pdf

paper.citation: di Prampero PE, Osgnach C. Metabolic Power in Team Sports - Part 1: An Update. International Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018;39:581-587.
paper.abstract: Team-sport energy expenditure is estimated from GPS speed and acceleration by treating accelerated running as uphill running, and the update includes walking and air resistance. The updated model gives whole-match energy expenditure about 14% lower than the original approach, with air resistance about 2% of the total. The paper is theoretical and contains no new comparison with measured values.
paper.tldr: A GPS-based model can estimate energy cost in team sports by treating accelerated running as uphill running, and the update separates walking from running. The authors' example suggests the earlier method overestimates match energy expenditure by about 14%.
paper.methods: Theoretical update of an existing model, with equations for the energy cost of running and walking on an equivalent slope, a walk-to-run transition speed, and an air-resistance term. An illustrative average 90-minute match from 497 Serie A players is used, with the data cited as in preparation.
paper.findings: In the example, air resistance accounts for about 1.7% of total energy expenditure and walking for about 25%. Treating all locomotion as running gives about 13.7% higher overall energy expenditure than the updated approach. The authors state that acceleration data need a sampling rate of at least 10 Hz, careful filtering and validation before the estimates are reliable.
paper.limitations: The authors say the approach omits jumps, backward running, ball carrying, kicking and contact, and that it uses a linear extrapolation beyond the slopes Minetti et al. measured. They also assume the same energy cost of level running and the same coefficients for all players, and acknowledge these assumptions may not hold for individuals.
paper.practicalImplications: The paper states that GPS acceleration data sampled below 10 Hz are highly questionable and that signal filtering and algorithms must be appropriately chosen and validated before the model is used. Practitioners should read the energy values as model estimates that depend on fixed assumptions for all players.
paper.athleteDev: The model may allow drills and matches to be compared by energy demand, including walking, running and air resistance, using only GPS speed and acceleration. Its outputs are estimates that assume the same energy cost for every player and ignore jumps, kicking and contact, so they should not be read as measured energy expenditure.
paper.rtp: The paper addresses match and training energetics and does not cover injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot inform return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Metabolic Power in Team Sports - Part 2- Aerobic and Anaerobic Energy Yields.pdf

paper.citation: Osgnach C, di Prampero PE. Metabolic Power in Team Sports - Part 2: Aerobic and Anaerobic Energy Yields. International Journal of Sports Medicine. 2018.
paper.abstract: A GPS-based method estimates metabolic power and oxygen uptake in team sports, and this paper tests it against a portable metabolic cart and reports aerobic and anaerobic energy yields. Estimated oxygen uptake was close to measured values on average but varied by protocol, and match data show fewer high-intensity efforts later in a soccer match.
paper.tldr: A GPS-based model estimated oxygen uptake fairly closely overall, but errors ranged from about 15% under to 20% over depending on the activity. Serie A match data suggest fewer high-intensity bouts later in the game, with longer low-intensity periods between them.
paper.methods: A preliminary set of shuttle-run data from 9 subjects and a later experiment (subject number not stated) compared model-estimated oxygen uptake with breath-by-breath measurement from a portable metabolic cart during walking, constant running and three sprint protocols (straight, L-shaped and shuttle), with blood lactate sampled. A separate analysis applies the model to match data from 497 outfield players in 71 Serie A matches, cited as in preparation.
paper.findings: Estimated oxygen uptake matched measured values for constant-speed walking, was about 20% higher for constant-speed running and about 15% lower for intermittent running. For one typical subject over a 47-minute trial, measured oxygen use was about 10% below estimated energy expenditure. In matches, the number of high-intensity bouts fell from 30 in the first 15 minutes to 23 in the last, with mean high-intensity power about 22 W/kg, while mean low-intensity power fell from about 5.8 to 4.8 W/kg.
paper.limitations: The model assumes the same energy cost and oxygen kinetics for all players and does not correct for individual differences, and measured resting oxygen uptake rose by about 46% over the session. Match data and the detailed validation analysis are cited as in preparation, so they cannot be checked from this paper.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest that low-intensity periods and the recovery between high-intensity bouts deserve as much attention as the high-intensity bouts themselves. Practitioners should keep in mind that estimated oxygen use is approximate and that pre-exercise oxygen uptake rises during a session.
paper.athleteDev: Match data in this paper suggest that high-intensity bouts become less frequent later in a match, with recovery between bouts lengthening, which may matter for late-game conditioning and recovery planning. The authors describe the estimates as reasonable but variable, so they are best used as approximate guides rather than exact physiological prescriptions.
paper.rtp: The study uses soccer match and sprint protocols and does not measure injury or return to play, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions.

records.sourceFile: Monitoring Dietary Supplements for Undeclared Diuretics as a Strategy for Preventing Unintentional Doping.pdf

paper.citation: Kozhuharov VR, Ivanov K, Ivanova S. Monitoring dietary supplements for undeclared diuretics as a strategy for preventing unintentional doping. Processes. 2025;13:79.
paper.abstract: This study developed and validated a gradient HPLC-UV method to screen dietary supplements for furosemide, torasemide and hydrochlorothiazide, as a way to reduce unintentional doping. Applied to 10 supplements, the method detected an undeclared diuretic (furosemide, 1210 µg per capsule) in one product.
paper.tldr: A low-cost HPLC-UV method can screen supplements for three diuretics, and it found undeclared furosemide in one of the 10 products tested. It is a laboratory screening method, and the paper does not show how often supplements used by athletes are contaminated.
paper.methods: Reversed-phase gradient HPLC with UV detection at 272 nm on a C18 column, with a 12-minute run. Validation followed ICH guidance for linearity, accuracy, precision, LOD and LOQ, and robustness (column temperature 32 to 38 °C). Ten randomly selected, purchased supplements, all promoted for weight loss and detoxification, and three diuretic medicines were analysed in triplicate, with spiked-recovery tests on two supplements.
paper.findings: Calibration was linear from 3.125 to 50 µg/mL (R2 above 0.999). Intra-day CVs were 0.18 to 1.48% and inter-day CVs were 0.52 to 2.04%, and recovery in spiked supplement samples was 95.5 to 102.7%. Of the 10 supplements, only Sample 6 contained an undeclared diuretic, furosemide at 1210 µg per capsule (about 2420 µg per day at the recommended two capsules). The product was a herbal supplement labelled with cassia tora, hawthorn and water lily leaves and advertised for weight loss.
paper.limitations: No athletes or human samples were tested, the products were weight-loss and detox supplements rather than sports supplements, and the nine other products showed no detected diuretic. The detection limits (0.69 to 0.99 µg/mL) are higher than those of LC-MS/MS, which the authors describe as more sensitive, and the paper reports no mass-spectrometry confirmation of the furosemide finding. The validation was carried out in a single laboratory with a small number of products.
paper.practicalImplications: Laboratories that check supplement quality can use this HPLC-UV method as a low-cost screen for furosemide, torasemide and hydrochlorothiazide. Teams that supply supplements to athletes should consider independent quality testing before use, since one of the 10 products here contained an undeclared diuretic. Because the method is less sensitive than LC-MS/MS, a negative screen should not be read as proof that a product is free of diuretics.
paper.athleteDev: The paper has no performance outcome. Its relevance for staff is supplement quality: the contaminated product was sold for weight loss, and the authors link undeclared diuretics to electrolyte imbalance, dehydration and unintentional anti-doping violations.
paper.rtp: Not applicable to return-to-sport decisions. The study has no athlete or patient sample and gives no guidance on medicine or supplement use during rehabilitation.

records.sourceFile: Monitoring external workload with wearable technology after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Golberg E, Pinkoski A, Beaupre L, Rouhani H. Monitoring external workload with wearable technology after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a scoping review. Orthop J Sports Med. 2023;11(8):23259671231191134.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA-ScR scoping review summarised 20 studies that used wearable technology to measure external workload after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). Accelerometers were the most common device, and daily steps and moderate to vigorous physical activity were the main outcomes, with deficits reported against healthy controls and between limbs in some studies.
paper.tldr: Wearable accelerometers can track daily activity after ACLR outside the clinic, and several studies found lower step counts or activity in ACLR groups than in controls. The evidence comes mostly from small cross-sectional studies, and the review found no evidence that these measures predict future ACL injury.
paper.methods: Scoping review following the Arksey and O'Malley framework, JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR. Eight databases were searched in February 2023, giving 2831 unique records after duplicates were removed; 175 full texts were reviewed and 20 included. A single reviewer screened titles and abstracts, two reviewers did full-text selection and extraction (agreement 91.39%, Cohen's kappa 0.66), and no formal quality assessment was made.
paper.findings: Daily step count from accelerometers or pedometers was the most common outcome (15 studies), and MVPA was reported in 10. Several studies found fewer daily steps or less MVPA in ACLR groups than controls, others found no difference, and adolescents with ACLR had 26% fewer daily steps and 33% less MVPA than adults with ACLR. Plantar insoles in one study showed lower daily loading of the surgical limb than the non-surgical limb (d = 0.63, P < .001), elite rugby players with ACLR covered less match distance than controls in one study, and MVPA was not associated with new or recurrent ACL injury in one follow-up study.
paper.limitations: No quality appraisal was conducted, and the review did not assess the validity or reliability of the outcomes it lists, although the authors state that the devices have acceptable criterion validity for step counting and activity monitoring. Most of the 20 studies were cross-sectional, several had very small groups, and most participants were physically active rather than competitive athletes (23% athletes, 1% elite). Most of the evidence comes from accelerometers, with only one GPS study and one insole study.
paper.practicalImplications: Wearable accelerometers can give rehabilitation teams step and activity data from daily life over periods that a single clinic test cannot cover. The authors advise caution when interpreting these outcomes because their validity and reliability after ACLR were not assessed. Use them alongside clinical return-to-sport testing rather than in place of it, because the review found no evidence that they predict future ACL injury.
paper.athleteDev: The review covers activity and workload during rehabilitation rather than performance. It reports very little wearable data on training or competition after ACLR (only a few studies, including one case report and one rugby study), so it offers little evidence for sport-specific load decisions.
paper.rtp: Relevant to return to sport because the included studies measured activity from about 2 weeks to 5 years after ACLR, and some report between-limb asymmetry. The review does not set return-to-sport criteria, and it found no evidence that these measures predict future ACL injury, so they cannot support a clearance decision on their own.

records.sourceFile: More than metrics - The role of socio-environmental factors in determining the success of athlete monitoring.pdf

paper.citation: Neupert E, Holder T, Gupta L, Jobson SA. More than metrics: The role of socio-environmental factors in determining the success of athlete monitoring. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2024.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional survey asked 30 UK elite sport practitioners (a 40% response from 75 invited) how they rated their athlete monitoring systems. Practitioners were divided on whether their athlete self-report measures were sensitive, and a scientific basis for the measures was linked to feedback to athletes and to stakeholder responsiveness. Socio-environmental factors such as buy-in and feedback were highlighted alongside metric quality.
paper.tldr: Practitioners were split on whether their self-report measures were sensitive, and about half thought performance would suffer without monitoring. Feedback to athletes was associated with adherence, so the social side of monitoring needs as much attention as the metrics.
paper.methods: Online closed survey, completed in 2017/18, sent to 75 practitioners working with tier 3 to 5 Olympic and Paralympic athletes in the UK; 30 responded, and most (83%, n = 25) used a custom system. Likert and checkbox items were analysed with Spearman correlations and a Bonferroni-corrected alpha of 0.017, and free-text answers were grouped into themes.
paper.findings: Fifty-two percent (n = 13) were confident in the sensitivity of their athlete self-report measures, and 64% (n = 16) said the measures had a scientific underpinning. A scientific underpinning correlated with feedback to athletes (rS(23) = 0.487, p = 0.014) and feedback correlated with athlete adherence (rS(22) = 0.675, p < 0.001); the link to confidence (rS(23) = 0.398, p = 0.049) did not meet the corrected threshold and is described as a trend. Fifty-two percent (n = 13) felt performance might be compromised without monitoring, while 56% (n = 14) had worked with internationally successful athletes who did not complete it.
paper.limitations: Only 30 of 75 invited practitioners responded, the sample is UK-based and self-selected, and the data are perceptions from 2017/18, so non-response bias is likely and the correlations do not show causation. Several percentages match a denominator of 23 to 25 rather than 30, and the discussion gives 58% for the item the results report as 56%.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff who doubt that their self-report measures are scientifically grounded should review the evidence behind them, because the survey linked a scientific basis to feedback to athletes. Adherence planning should include what athletes are told about their data, since feedback was correlated with adherence, and coach buy-in should be treated as part of the system, not a separate issue.
paper.athleteDev: The study suggests that monitoring value depends on feedback to athletes and on coach buy-in as well as on the metric. The correlations do not show whether better feedback causes better adherence.
paper.rtp: The study did not measure injury, rehabilitation or return to sport, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions or the choice of a return-to-play measure.

records.sourceFile: Motion Capture Technologies for Athletic Performance Enhancement and Injury Risk Assessment - A Review for Multi-Sport Organizations.pdf

paper.citation: Adlou B, Wilburn C, Weimar W. Motion Capture Technologies for Athletic Performance Enhancement and Injury Risk Assessment: A Review for Multi-Sport Organizations. Sensors. 2025;25:4384.
paper.abstract: This review compares optical marker-based, inertial (IMU) and markerless motion capture for athlete use across indoor court, aquatic and outdoor field settings. It draws on peer-reviewed studies from 2015 to 2025, 82 of 234 full-text articles, and proposes a phased purchasing framework for multi-sport organizations.
paper.tldr: Each motion capture technology trades accuracy against practicality: optical systems are most accurate in the lab, while IMU and markerless systems suit field and team use but with larger errors. Verify accuracy on the sport's own movements before buying, rather than relying on vendor claims.
paper.methods: Narrative review of PubMed, SPORTDiscus and Web of Science searches (January 2015 to January 2025) using motion capture and validation keywords. Of 953 unique articles, 234 were screened at full text and 82 met the eligibility criteria, which covered validation, comparative and implementation studies; no formal risk-of-bias appraisal or pooled analysis is reported.
paper.findings: Optical systems were sub-millimeter accurate in controlled settings, but IMU joint-angle errors varied widely: Xsens RMSEs were about 3 to 10 degrees for knee, ankle and hip in walking and running, while APDM Opal RMSEs in jumps, squats, lunges and cuts were 8.11 to 28.37 degrees sagittal and up to 116.75 degrees transverse. Theia3D markerless sagittal RMSEs were 3.20 to 15.66 degrees, and GNSS-integrated IMU units had positional accuracy of about 0.3 m under optimal conditions, which degraded in stadiums with high stands. Waterproof IMU orientation error was 6.1 degrees in water versus 4.4 degrees dry, and cited studies reported 99.7 to 100% lap-counting accuracy.
paper.limitations: The review applies no formal quality appraisal. Its abstract states IMU angular accuracy of 2 to 8 degrees, but in the body that figure is attributed to Xsens MVN multi-sensor validation studies, while other cited IMU validations report much larger joint-angle errors in some joints, planes and dynamic tasks. The authors note that most validation samples were male and that long-term reliability data are lacking, so accuracy figures are ranges across studies rather than guarantees for any one system.
paper.practicalImplications: Organizations should match validation evidence to their own sports and movements rather than to vendor specifications, which the review says can differ substantially from field performance. Its foundation phase is either a team IMU system for workload or a multi-camera markerless system for controlled technique analysis, with optical systems added later for research or clinical work.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, the review pairs a team IMU or GNSS system for workload with a markerless system for technique analysis. Because joint-angle errors can be large for some movements and planes, the review advises conservative interpretation thresholds so that differences within known measurement error are not read as real change.
paper.rtp: The review suggests a multi-sensor IMU system and a mid-range optical system for return-to-play validation, but it tests no injured athletes and reports no return-to-play outcomes. It cannot show that these systems detect return-to-play readiness, which would need validation in the injury-relevant movements.

records.sourceFile: Moving beyond velocity derivatives - Using GPS data to extract sequential movement patterns at different levels of rugby league match-play.pdf

paper.citation: Collins N, White R, Palczewska A, Weaving D, Dalton-Barron N, Jones B. Moving beyond velocity derivatives; Using Global Positioning System data to extract sequential movement patterns at different levels of rugby league match-play. European Journal of Sport Science. 2022.
paper.abstract: This observational study applied the sequential movement pattern (SMP) framework to GPS data from 11 rugby league matches at three competition levels. It identified 121 movement patterns, mostly built from walk and jog units, and nine of 17 movement units differed between levels, mainly between international and regular Super League matches.
paper.tldr: A movement-pattern method applied to GPS data shows that rugby league match play is built mostly from low-speed walk and jog actions, and these differ most between international and regular Super League matches. The study describes match demands; it does not test whether training to match these patterns changes outcomes.
paper.methods: Observational analysis of 2019 GPS data (Catapult Optimeye S5, 10 Hz) from 11 matches, covering four regular Super League, three semi-finals or finals and four international matches. Movement patterns were tested with linear discriminant analysis (accuracy 0.81), and the 17 movement units used in the patterns were compared with Kruskal-Wallis tests, Dunn post-hoc tests and Cohen's d effect sizes.
paper.findings: The framework found 121 movement patterns, and no pattern was unique to one competition level. Nine of 17 movement units differed between levels: all nine differed between international and regular Super League matches, three differed between international and finals, and four differed between the two domestic levels. The authors report that the units that differed were mainly low velocity, and that walk and jog patterns were the most prevalent.
paper.limitations: The sample is small (11 matches), and the international data come from a single team set against several domestic teams, so tactics and squad differences may explain the results as much as competition level. The authors' claim of more high-velocity patterns in international matches (units T, S and y) is descriptive, since those units showed no significant difference (p = 1.000), and the conclusion overstates the domestic comparison because only three units differed from the finals. Match outcome and context were not analysed, and the text cites unit h as significant although Table 1 has no row for it.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff preparing players for rugby league could use movement-pattern analysis to check whether training includes the walk and jog sequences, with their acceleration and turning changes, that occur in match play, rather than relying on total distance or speed bands alone. Any move toward more high-speed work for international preparation should await a study that links these patterns to outcomes, because the high-velocity claim here is descriptive.
paper.athleteDev: The study suggests that movement sequences, not only speed thresholds, can describe match demands and differ by competition level. The authors infer that international players need more high-speed exposure, but that inference rests on descriptive counts and was not tested.
paper.rtp: The study covers match demands in players and does not include injury, rehabilitation or return to play, so it cannot guide return-to-play decisions. Any use in return-to-play planning would be the reader's inference, since no injured players were studied.

records.sourceFile: Myostatin inhibitory peptides in sports drug testing.pdf

paper.citation: Walpurgis K, Agricola J, Thomas A, Thevis M. Myostatin inhibitory peptides in sports drug testing. Drug Test Anal. 2023.
paper.abstract: Myostatin inhibitors are potential muscle-building agents and are prohibited under section S4 of the WADA Prohibited List. The authors developed and characterized a protein precipitation and LC-HRMS/MS method to detect six myostatin inhibitory peptides in doping control serum, with detection down to 3 to 9 ng/mL, and identified possible metabolites of DF-3, DF-25 and Peptide 7 as complementary targets.
paper.tldr: An anti-doping lab built and validated a blood test for six experimental myostatin-blocking peptides that are not clinically approved but can be bought for research. It shows the assay works on spiked samples; how long real use stays detectable is still unknown.
paper.methods: Six custom-synthesized peptides and two internal standards were measured in serum after acidification and acetonitrile protein precipitation, using an Orbitrap LC-HRMS/MS system. Selectivity, linearity, detection limit, recovery, carryover, matrix effects, robustness in plasma and stability were assessed per WADA guidelines with commercial serum and samples from 10 healthy volunteers, and metabolites were sought after 2 h incubation of each peptide in serum.
paper.findings: No interfering signals were found in 10 blank sera, responses were linear to 100 ng/mL (r above 0.97), and estimated detection limits were 3 to 9 ng/mL. Recovery was 20% to 48% for most peptides but about 8% for Peptide 8a. At room temperature Peptide 7, DF-3 and DF-25 degraded within 1 h while Peptide 8a was detectable for 14 days, and N-terminally shortened metabolites were found for Peptides 7 and 3d, DF-3 and DF-25.
paper.limitations: All validation used fortified serum or plasma; the peptides are in preclinical development and have not been tested in humans, so authentic post-administration samples were not available to confirm sensitivity, detection windows or in vivo metabolites. Several targets were unstable in serum even when refrigerated, and the identified metabolites were also unstable, which may limit detection after sample transport.
paper.practicalImplications: For anti-doping education, the paper documents that myostatin inhibitory peptides are prohibited, are sold for research and on the black market, and are now targeted by a validated serum assay. It gives no evidence of performance benefit or safety in humans.
paper.athleteDev: Does not measure performance. Muscle mass and strength gains cited for these peptides come from mouse studies described in the introduction, not from this study.
paper.rtp: Not relevant to return to sport. It is a laboratory detection method and cannot inform injury management or clearance decisions.

paper.citation: Retzky JS, Koff MF, Nwawka OK, Rodeo SA. Novel Noninvasive Imaging Techniques to Assess Structural, Functional, and Material Properties of Tendon, Ligament, and Cartilage: A Narrative Review of Current Concepts. Orthop J Sports Med. 2025;13(2):23259671251317223.
paper.abstract: Narrative review of quantitative MRI (qMRI) and shear wave elastography (SWE) for soft tissue of the knee and shoulder, including meniscus, ACL graft, articular cartilage and rotator cuff. A PubMed search was run in October 2022 using four keyword phrases, and clinical studies and reviews were included. The authors report that qMRI and SWE may improve early detection of pathology and help evaluate tissue after treatment, while conventional MRI and ultrasound have limited ability to assess material properties.
paper.tldr: Quantitative MRI and shear wave elastography can measure soft tissue composition and stiffness that standard MRI and ultrasound do not show, with early uses in ACL graft maturity, meniscal healing and cartilage degeneration. The evidence is mostly early-stage, animal-based or small, and the authors say these tools are not yet established for routine clinical decisions.
paper.methods: The authors call this a narrative review, but it describes a database search, so the library codes it as a systematic review by precedent. A PubMed search was performed in October 2022 with four keyword phrases (quantitative MRI tendon, ligament and cartilage, and shear wave elastography tendon). Cohort studies, systematic and narrative reviews, book chapters and randomized trials on clinical applications were included, editorials and technique papers were excluded, and no screening counts or quality appraisal are reported.
paper.findings: The review describes T2 mapping and UTE-T2* imaging for ACL graft maturity, with one human study reporting that UTE-T2* values changed mostly in the first 6 months and decreased between 1 and 2 years after reconstruction. In a goat meniscal repair model, T1rho relaxation times were sensitive to healing, and in a human cohort a T2 decrease of 22.3 ms was associated with complete healing confirmed by second-look arthroscopy. For SWE, torn tendons were reported to be softer, and in a pilot study Achilles stiffness rose at 6 weeks, plateaued, then rose again at 3 to 6 months after rupture, but the authors note that SWE was not associated with rotator cuff tear size, retraction or fatty infiltration in one study.
paper.limitations: The authors identify variability between MRI hardware and software, magic-angle effects, and contrast-agent concerns for qMRI. For SWE they note user dependence, sensitivity to patient position, sex and age, reduced reliability beyond about 7 cm depth, and cutoff values that differ between ultrasound systems. The review does not appraise study quality or sample sizes, and it cites a human meniscal pilot (Sneag) that found no significant T2* difference between repaired and meniscectomy groups. Several authors report industry ties, including a research agreement with GE Healthcare and Siemens Healthineers and consulting fees from Samsung.
paper.practicalImplications: Treat qMRI and SWE as research-stage tools for staff discussions, not as a basis for graft, meniscus or tendon clearance decisions. If a team considers SWE for tendon monitoring, the same operator, machine, transducer and positioning protocol should be used at each time point, because the authors report that these factors change readings.
paper.athleteDev: The review offers no performance outcomes or athlete-specific measurement norms. The tendon stiffness example in a college basketball player is illustrative only, so staff should not use these measures to set training loads.
paper.rtp: The review suggests that qMRI could help judge ACL graft maturity and meniscal healing, and SWE could help judge tendon healing, which may inform rehabilitation timing. It does not provide return-to-sport criteria or validated cutoffs, so these measures should not be used alone to clear an athlete to return to play.
